summary: Describes the RTP payload format for the Tactical Secure Voice Cryptographic Interoperability Specification speech coder, a scalable narrowband voice coder built as an augmentation of MELPe.

eli5.summary: Rules for putting scrambled radio-style voice into network packets.

questions: how is tsvcis carried in rtp
what is the tsvcis sdp tcmax parameter
subtitle: How to put TSVCIS tactical voice frames, built on the MELPe vocoder, into RTP packets.

tldr.problem: The TSVCIS speech coder adds extra speech parameters on top of the MELPe vocoder, and there was no agreed way to carry those frames in RTP packets or describe them in SDP.
tldr.mechanism: Each frame is a MELPe 2400 bps frame followed by byte-packed TSVCIS parameters and one or two trailing bytes that carry rate code bits and a count. Packets need no payload-specific header, and SDP parameters (bitrate, tcmax) negotiate the options.
tldr.outcome: Senders and receivers can interoperate, and links with little bandwidth can fall back to plain MELPe rates. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is not obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 8817 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2020. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and IANA has registered the TSVCIS media type.

sections.title: What TSVCIS Is and Why It Needs a Payload Format
sections.content:
RFC 8817 describes how compressed speech from the Tactical Secure Voice Cryptographic Interoperability Specification (TSVCIS) codec is formatted as an RTP payload. TSVCIS is a scalable narrowband voice coder. It augments the MELPe (Mixed Excitation Linear Prediction Enhanced) coder with extra speech parameters that improve voice quality.

The sender or any TSVCIS-aware equipment on the path can adapt to restricted bandwidth by sending less augmented data and relying on plain MELPe on the most constrained links. A packet may carry one or more codec frames, depending on network conditions, bandwidth limits, delay needs and loss tolerance.
sections.eli5: TSVCIS is a way of squeezing voice into very small messages. This RFC explains how to put those messages into network packets.

sections.title: Background: MELP, MELPe and TSVCIS
sections.content:
MELP was developed by the US military as an upgrade from the LPC-based CELP standard vocoder for low-bitrate communications. It was further enhanced and adopted by NATO as MELPe, international standard STANAG 4591. TSVCIS is a specification from the Tactical Secure Voice Working Group meant to make modern tactical secure voice devices interoperable across the US Department of Defense. Its voice modes are based on specific fixed rates of the Naval Research Lab's Variable Date Rate (VDR) Vocoder, which uses MELPe as its base.

A complete TSVCIS speech frame is MELPe speech parameters plus matching TSVCIS augmented speech data. The TSVCIS specification also says which bits get encrypted and how forward error correction protects them, but at the RTP layer only the speech coder bits matter, and they are carried unencrypted. The RFC notes that most IP deployments would secure the RTP contents with standard link encryption such as SRTP, VPNs, FIPS 140 link encryptors or Type 1 Ethernet encryptors.

The TSVCIS parameters are byte-packed. A three-bit field goes in the lowest bits of an octet, followed by the next five-bit field, and a parameter split between octets has its most significant bits in the earlier octet. Unfilled bits in the last octet MUST be zero. The VDR is used in two configurations with a fixed set of 15 and 35 packed octet parameters.
sections.eli5: Think of MELPe as a basic recipe for squeezing voice, and TSVCIS as extra seasoning that makes it taste better when there is room. The extra bits are packed tightly, with any leftover space filled with zeros.

sections.title: The RTP Payload and MELPe Frame Layouts
sections.content:
TSVCIS augments the MELP 2400, 1200 and 600 bitrates, so frames last 22.5, 67.5 or 90 ms, with an 8 kHz clock. The RTP timestamp MUST therefore be in units of 1/8000 of a second. No payload-specific header is needed: the payload is just one or more TSVCIS frames after the normal RTP header. When a packet holds several frames, the timestamp is that of the oldest frame.

MELPe packetization follows RFC 8130, with its recommendations now treated as requirements. The bits previously labeled RSVA, RSVB and RSVC are filled with rate code bits CODA, CODB and CODC. The rate code identifies the frame type and thus its length:

  • 2400 bps: 54 bits in 7 octets; CODA is 0 and CODB is 0.
  • 1200 bps: 81 bits in 11 octets; CODA, CODB and CODC are 1, 0, 0.
  • 600 bps: 54 bits in 7 octets; CODA is 0 and CODB is 1.
  • Comfort noise: 13 bits in 2 octets; CODA, CODB and CODC are 1, 0, 1.
  • TSVCIS data: CODA and CODB are both 1, with a variable length.

For 2400 and 600 bps, CODB SHOULD have the listed value but MAY carry an end-to-end framing bit if the endpoints need one. The M bit usage SHOULD follow the applicable RTP profile. Assigning a payload type is outside the scope of the RFC: a profile is expected to assign one, and otherwise the sender picks one from the dynamic range.
sections.eli5: Each little voice message starts with a couple of marker bits that say what kind it is, so the receiver knows how long it is. The markers work like colored stickers on envelopes.

sections.title: Packing TSVCIS Data and Multiple Frames
sections.content:
TSVCIS packed parameters MUST come immediately after a matching MELPe 2400 bps payload in the same RTP packet. There are two layouts, both ending in trailing bytes that start with CODA and CODB both set to one.

  • Preferred placement (SHOULD be used when the parameter octet count TC is 77 or less): one trailing octet holds the two rate bits and a six-bit modified count, MTC = TC - 15. The standard implementation uses at least 15 octets, and the largest MTC is 62, which gives 77. The all-ones value 63 SHALL NOT be used here because it signals the alternate format.
  • Alternate placement (for all other VDR configurations): two trailing bytes. The last has CODA, CODB and six one bits. The second-to-last holds the octet count TC from 1 to 255, with 0 reserved.

A packet holds zero or more consecutive TSVCIS frames, oldest first, then zero or one MELPe comfort noise frame. An empty packet MAY be sent periodically to show connectivity from an otherwise idle sender. Frames in one packet MAY have different TSVCIS parameter counts, but all MELPe frames in one packet MUST have the same coder bitrate. Senders SHOULD NOT put more frames in a packet than fit in the MTU, and frames MUST NOT be split between packets.

The packet does not say how many frames it holds. The receiver finds out by walking through the packet, identifying each frame's type and length from the rate codes.
sections.eli5: After the basic voice piece comes an optional extra-detail piece, then a label at the end saying how big the extra piece is. A packet can hold several of these in a row, and the receiver counts them by reading each label.

sections.title: Media Type and SDP Parameters
sections.content:
The payload format is registered as media type audio/TSVCIS with a required clock rate of 8000 Hz and one channel. Optional parameters are:

  • ptime and maxptime: packet durations rounded up to whole milliseconds (23, 45, 68, 90, 112, 135, 156 and 180 for TSVCIS).
  • bitrate: a comma-separated list from 2400, 1200 and 600, in order of preference. If absent, the fixed rate 2400 MUST be used.
  • tcmax: the maximum TC supported or wanted, from 1 to 255. The default is 35.

In SDP, the encoding name is TSVCIS, and bitrate and tcmax go in the a=fmtp line. The RFC says ptime cannot select the operating mode, because for example 68 ms could mean one 67.5 ms frame or three 22.5 ms frames.

For declarative SDP, several payload types may each advertise a different bitrate. In offer/answer (RFC 3264), both sides MUST use a common bitrate, and the first bitrate in the answer is the initial one. If the offer says 2400,600 and the answer says 600,2400, the initial bitrate is 600. For tcmax, both sides SHOULD use a common value, and the answerer MAY pick a value equal to or less than the offered one or ignore augmented data it cannot use.
sections.eli5: Before talking, the two sides agree on how fast to send and how much extra detail to include. They do it by listing what they can handle, and the answerer's first choice wins.

sections.title: Congestion, Silence and Packet Loss
sections.content:
The TSVCIS target bitrate can change at any time, and so can the amount of speech per packet, which helps with congestion control. A lower packet rate reduces header overhead but raises latency and loss sensitivity. Because UDP offers no congestion control, applications using RTP over UDP SHOULD implement their own and MAY use a transport circuit breaker.

Discontinuous transmission is normal for radio-style voice. Sequence number gaps mean lost packets to be filled by packet loss concealment (PLC), while an abrupt stop of packets means an intended pause. Resumed speech SHOULD set the RTP marker bit to 1. A coder may send a MELPe comfort noise frame before it stops, and no SDP negotiation is needed.

For PLC, an erasure is signaled with an errored encoding of a non-voiced frame; the preferred pitch/voicing value is 3 (bits P0 and P1 set to one, P2 to P6 zero). In 1200 or 600 bps mode, the MELPe 2400 bps decoder is called three or four times respectively to cover one lost low-rate frame.
sections.eli5: If a few packets get lost, the receiver patches the gap with a made-up sound so you do not hear a hole. If the sender just stops, that means nobody is talking.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The payload inherits the security considerations of RTP and of the profile in use (RTP/AVP, AVPF, SAVP or SAVPF). The RFC says choosing mechanisms for confidentiality, integrity and source authentication is the job of whoever uses RTP, and applications SHOULD use appropriate strong security mechanisms.

As far as the authors know, the format does not make receiver-side processing cost vary much, so pathological data is unlikely to be a denial-of-service threat, and the payload carries no active content. For the effect of voice activity detection on bitrates, the RFC points to the guidance in RFC 6562.
sections.eli5: The packing rules are not dangerous by themselves. Keeping the call secret is the job of the lock you put on the whole network connection.

items.label: 2400 bps
items.desc: CODA, CODB, CODC (- means N/A). 7 octets.

viz.caption: TWO TRAILER LAYOUTS FOR TSVCIS DATA

items.title: Preferred
items.text: TC up to 77 octets. One trailing octet: CODA, CODB and a 6-bit MTC = TC - 15. MTC 63 is not allowed.

items.title: Alternate
items.text: Any TC from 1 to 255. Two trailing bytes: the octet count, then CODA, CODB and six one bits.
